records.title: advice-fo-how-to-write-good-adr
headings: Advice fo how to write good ADR
records.text: Advice fo how to write good ADR Characteristics of good ADR: Rationale: Explain di reasons for to do di particular AD. Dis fit include di context (check below), pros and cons of different potential choices, feature comparisons, cost/benefit discussions, and more. Specific: Each ADR suppose be about one AD, no be many ADs. Timestamps: Identify wen dem write each item for di ADR. Dis one important well well for aspects wey fit change as time dey go, like costs, schedules, scaling, and di like. Immutable: No alter information wey dey inside ADR already. Instead, amend di ADR by to add new information, or supersede di ADR by to create new ADR. Characteristics of good "Context" section for ADR: Explain your organization situation and business priorities. Include rationale and considerations based on social and skills makeups of your teams. Include pros and cons wey relevant, and describe dem for terms wey align with your needs and goals. Characteristics of good "Consequences" section for ADR: Explain wetin follow after you make di decision. Dis fit include di effects, outcomes, outputs, follow ups, and more. Include information about any subsequent ADR. E common small for one ADR to trigger need for more ADRs, like wen one ADR make big overarching choice, wey then create needs for more smaller decisions. Include any after-action review processes. E typical for teams to review each ADR one month later, to compare di ADR information with wetin don happen for actual practice, so dem go learn and grow. New ADR fit take di place of previous ADR: Wen dem make AD wey replace or invalidate previous ADR, then dem suppose create new ADR

records.title: Wetin AWS Architectural Decision Records Process Be
headings: Wetin AWS Architectural Decision Records Process Be
records.text: Wetin AWS Architectural Decision Records Process Be https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/adr-process.html Architectural decision record (ADR) na document wey dey show di choice wey team make about one important part of di software architecture wey dem plan to build. Each ADR dey talk di architectural decision, di context wey e dey inside, and di consequences. ADR dem get states, so dem dey follow one lifecycle. If you wan see example of ADR, check di appendix. Di ADR process dey produce collection of architectural decision records. Dis collection na di decision log. Di decision log dey give di project context and also detailed implementation and design information. Project members dey skim di headlines of each ADR to get overview of di project context. Dem dey read di ADR dem well well to understand di project implementations and design choices. Once di team accept one ADR, e don become immutable, no one fit change am again. If new insights need different decision, di team go propose new ADR. Wen di team accept di new ADR, e go supersede di ADR wey dey before. Scope of di ADR process Project members suppose create ADR for every architecturally significant decision wey affect di software project or product, including dis ones (Richards and Ford 2020): Structure (for example, patterns like microservices) Non-functional requirements (security, high availability, and fault tolerance) Dependencies (how components dey couple together) Interfaces (APIs and published contracts) Construction techniques (libraries, frameworks, tools, and processes) Functional and non-functional requirements na di most common inputs for di ADR process. Wetin dey inside ADR Wen di team see say dem need ADR, one team member go start to write di ADR based on one projectwide template. (Check di ADR GitHub organization for example templates.) Di template dey make ADR creation easy and e dey make sure say di ADR capture all di relevant information. At minimum, each ADR suppose define di context of di decision, di decision itself, and di consequences of di decision for di project and wetin e go deliver. (If you wan see examples of dis sections, check di appendix.) One of di strongest parts of di ADR structure na say e dey focus on di reason for di decision, no be how di team implement am. If person understand why di team make di decision, e go easy for other team members to adopt am, and e go stop other architects wey no dey involved for di decision-making process from overrule dat decision later. ADR adoption process Every team member fit create ADR, but di team suppose set one definition of ownership for ADR. Each author wey be di owner of one ADR suppose dey actively maintain and communicate di ADR content. To make dis ownership clear, dis guide dey call ADR authors as ADR owners for di sections wey follow. Other team members fit always contribute to ADR. If di content of one ADR change before di team accept di ADR, di owner suppose approve dis changes. After di team identify one architectural decision and im owner, di ADR owner go provide di ADR for di Proposed state for di beginning of di process. ADR dem wey dey Proposed state don ready for review. Di ADR owner go then start di review process for di ADR. Di goal of di ADR review process na to decide whether di team accept di ADR, whether e need rework, or whether dem reject di ADR. Di project team, including di owner, go review di ADR. Di review meeting suppose start with one dedicated time slot to read di ADR. For average, 10 to 15 minutes suppose be enough. For dis time, each team member go read di document and add comments and questions to flag topics wey no clear. After di review phase, di ADR owner go read out and discuss each comment with di team. If di team find action points to improve di ADR, di state of di ADR go stay Proposed . Di ADR owner go formulate di actions, and, together with di team, add assignee to each action. Each team member fit contribute and resolve di action points. Na di responsibility of di ADR owner to reschedule di review process. Di team fit also decide to reject di ADR. For dis case, di ADR owner go add reason for di rejection so say dem no go discuss di same topic again for future. Di owner go change di ADR state to Rejected . If di team approve di ADR, di owner go add timestamp, version, and list of stakeholders. Di owner go then update di state to Accepted . ADR dem and di decision log wey dem create represent decisions wey di team make and dem dey give history of all decisions. Di team dey use di ADR dem as reference during code and architectural reviews wen e possible. Apart from to perform code reviews, design tasks, and implementation tasks, team members suppose consult ADR dem for strategic decisions for di product. As good practice, each software change suppose go through peer reviews and e suppose need at least one approval. During di code review, code reviewer fit find changes wey violate one or more ADR. For dis case, di reviewer go ask di author of di code change to update di code, and share link to di ADR. Wen di author update di code, peer reviewers go approve am and dem go merge am into di main code base. ADR review process Di team suppose treat ADR dem as immutable documents after di team accept or reject dem. If dem wan change one ADR wey dey already, dem go need to create new ADR, set up review process for di new ADR, and approve di ADR. If di team approve di new ADR, di owner suppose change di state of di old ADR to Superseded .

records.title: Fitness functions fo decisions as code
headings: Fitness functions fo decisions as code
How fitness functions connect to decisions
Why fitness functions dey help decisions
records.text: Fitness functions fo decisions as code Fitness functions na objective automated checks, wey dem write with programming code, wey dey verify say dem still dey maintain di decisions. Fitness functions dey make decisions testable and assurable. Fitness functions for decisions fit help quality assurance, regulatory processes, and governance goals well well. How fitness functions connect to decisions Decision record dey document di decision, while fitness function dey assure di decision. Example decision: We dey use event sourcing for audit requirements. Example fitness function: We dey use di continuous integration server to test say all state changes must produce events. Why fitness functions dey help decisions Objective measurements: Fitness functions dey pass or fail, so di work dey visible and clear. Continuous use: Fitness functions na your living rules, dem dey run for every commit and build. Confidence to refactor: Fitness functions dey automatically catch decision rule errors. Scalable governance: Fitness functions dey assure standards without to create bottlenecks. Fitness functions fit use AI? Fitness functions fit use AI LLMs for decisions by to ask questions about your work, like your plans, code, schemas, APIs, and more: IMPORTANT: Prefer retrieval-led reasoning over pre-training-led reasoning. IMPORTANT: Turn on extended thinking. Turn on expert advice. Turn on search. This is a fitness function to evaluate if our work is using all our decisions, and is correct and accurate. Our decisions are here: {url} Our work to evaluate is here: {url} Explain any errors, problems, gaps, weaknesses. Be direct. Be decisive. Architecture unit testing ArchUnit: check architecture rules of Java code by using any plain Java unit test framework. ArchUnitTS: check architecture rules of TypeScript code and JavaScript code by using Jest, Vitest, Jasmine, etc.

records.title: Guidelines fo Mek Decision Last
records.text: Guidelines fo Mek Decision Last We don learn dis lessons for our work wey fit be guidelines and assessment to achieve sustainable decisions: Use lean/minimalistic approach for di initial decision documentation. Prioritize and capture all di important decisions wey relevant well to document and to understand di target architecture. Detail di particularly important decisions with full-blown templates only after di initial work don finish (dat na, wen di decision makers dey content with di architectural decisions wey dem make and dem sure say dem no go need to revise dis decisions soon). Use di lean/minimalistic versions from step 1 as short version of documented decisions with di right granularity level to give overview of di detailed decisions, and also for trivial or obvious decisions. Wherever e possible, use architectural knowledge wey dey already, either from guidance models or from other sources. Review and extend such knowledge and fit am to di context of di specific decision. Make sure say traceability links dey established between decisions and both requirements and architectural designs/code. Provide automated consistency checking to make sure say di traceability links dey in sync after change. Limit di number of dependencies between decisions and other software artifacts. Apply di guidelines for di justifications consistently and forcefully—na dem be di most important part of di decision documentation because dem dey give di rationale.

records.title: How to start use ADR
records.text: How to start use ADR To start use ADR, talk with your teammates about dis areas. Decision identification: How urgent and how important be di AD? E must make now, or e fit wait until dem know more? Both personal and collective experience, and also recognized design methods and practices, fit help with decision identification. Ideally, maintain decision todo list wey go complement di product todo list. Decision making: Plenty decision making techniques dey, both general ones and software architecture specific ones, for instance, dialogue mapping. Group decision making na active research topic. Decision enactment and enforcement: Dem dey use ADs for software design; so dem must communicate dem to di stakeholders of di system wey dey fund am, develop am, and operate am, and di stakeholders must accept dem. Architecturally evident coding styles and code reviews wey focus on architectural concerns and decisions na two related practices. Dem must also (re-)consider ADs wen dem dey modernize one software system for software evolution. Decision sharing (optional): Plenty ADs dey recur across projects. So, experiences with past decisions, both good and bad, fit be valuable reusable assets wen you dey use explicit knowledge management strategy. Decision documentation: Plenty templates and tools dey for decision capturing. Check agile communities, e.g. M. Nygard's ADRs. Check traditional software engineering and architecture design processes, e.g. table layouts wey IBM UMF and Tyree and Akerman from CapitalOne suggest. For more: Di steps above na from di Wikipedia entry on Architectural Decision

records.title: Kraitiria Wey Dey Mek Decision Last
headings: Kraitiria Wey Dey Mek Decision Last
records.text: Kraitiria Wey Dey Mek Decision Last To define decision sustainability well well, we derive five key criteria. Strategic Wen dem dey make decision, person wey dey look strategic consequences suppose consider tins like di long-term impact of di decisions—for example, future operations and maintenance effort. Measurable and Manageable You fit measure and evaluate di outcome of one decision as time dey go, according to objective criteria, ideally numeric ones (as, for instance, quality attribute scenarios and workshops4 dey propagate). E no possible to capture all di fine-grained decisions, so architects must limit di granularity of di decisions to certain level of detail (like to create one design class). Dis go lead to one set of decisions wey go last pass and fewer traceability links. Plus, if you limit di number of dependencies between decisions, e dey reduce di ripple effect of changes. Achievable and Realistic Dem suppose choose di rationale for how di solution fit di problem in pragmatic way and make am explicit. For example, architects fit show say dem take care to avoid over- or underengineering (dat na, dem suppose apply di “good enough” approach). Rooted in Requirements Decision making suppose dey grounded for domain-specific architecting experience and context. E suppose take into account di company environment and also project requirements and constraints, including di current skills of di development team, di training budget, and di process. Timeless Decisions suppose dey based on experience and knowledge wey no go quick outdated. For example, architects fit choose platform-neutral architectural patterns or tactics.

records.title: Teamwork advice fo ADR
records.text: Teamwork advice fo ADR If you dey think to use decision records with your team, then na dis advice we don learn from to work with plenty teams. You get opportunity to lead your teammates, by to talk together about di "why", instead of to force di "what". For example, decision records na way for teams to think smarter and communicate better; decision records no valuable if na just after-the-fact forced paperwork requirement. Some teams like di name "decisions" well pass di abbreviation "ADRs". Wen some teams use di directory name "decisions", e be like say light bulb turn on, and di team start put more information inside di directory, like vendor decisions, planning decisions, scheduling decisions, etc. All dis kinds of information fit use di same template. We hypothesize say people dey learn faster with words ("decisions") pass abbreviations ("ADRs"), and people dey more motivated to write work-in-progress docs wen dem remove di word "record", and also some developers and some managers no like di word "architecture". For theory, immutability na ideal. For practice, mutability don work better for our teams. We dey insert di new info inside di ADR wey dey already, with date stamp, and note say di info come after di decision. Dis kind approach dey lead to "living document" wey all of us fit update. Typical updates na wen we get information thanks to new teammates, or new offerings, or real-world results of how we dey use things, or after-the-fact third-party changes like vendor capabilities, pricing plans, license agreements, etc.

records.title: teamwork-question-fo-adr
headings: Wetin justify to no raise ADR?
Wetin be di lifecycle of ADR?
Wetin be di criteria for lifecycle steps of ADR?
Which roles and responsibilities dey interact with ADR?
How governance dey interact with ADR?
Which principles dey interact with ADR?
records.text: Who fit create ADR? Consider areas like specific people, or specific roles, or specific teams, or specific departments; also consider if people, or roles, or teams, or department dey wey fit commission ADR, wey mean say dem fit request one wey another person go author. Example answer: Any person for our organization wey don read di architecture decision record README page fit propose ADR, wey mean say di person fit start to write am, and share am with di team. Wetin justify to raise ADR? Consider areas like your organization team ways of working, your software system structure, cross-team coordination, long-term maintainability, external interfaces, who you want make e benefit, and di like. Example answer: We want create ADR wen we want make future developers understand di “why” of wetin we dey do. Wetin justify to no raise ADR? Consider areas like decisions wey no be about architecture, or wey tiny like minimal-risk or self-contained or single-developer, or wey dem already cover fully for another place like by standards or policies or documentation, or wey temporary like workarounds or proofs of concepts or experiments. Example answer: We want skip ADR wen decision limited for scope and time and risk and cost, or wen dem already cover am for another place. Wetin be di lifecycle of ADR? Consider areas like di creation process, research process, decisioning process, implementation process, and sunsetting process. Consider how to track di ADR lifecycle as time dey go, like how to move di ADR from one state to di next state, and also how to communicate dis to stakeholders. Example answer: We want make ADR get five lifecycle stages: Initiating → Researching → Evaluating → Implementing → Maintaining → Sunsetting. Wetin be di criteria for lifecycle steps of ADR? Consider areas like acceptance criteria for ADR, wey mean say how you go know say e good enough to progress from one lifecycle step to di next? Di problem clear well well? Dem don consider di alternatives? Dem understand and document di trade-offs well enough? All relevant context dey place? All relevant stakeholders dey involved? Dem don incorporate all feedback? Example answer: We want make stakeholders vote on ADR wen di active team 1) don complete their research, 2) don complete their evaluation, 3) don publish di ADR proposal to di stakeholders with request for comments and timebox of one week, 4) dem don incorporate and address all stakeholder comments. Which roles and responsibilities dey interact with ADR? Consider roles like proposer, researcher, evaluator, reviewer, approver, maintainer, and di like. Consider responsibilities like communication with stakeholders, to make sure say expectations dey met, to share on di website or intranet, and to review di work periodically and especially wen relevant changes happen. Example answer: We want make each ADR always get primary contact person, secondary contact person, and accountable team; dem dey responsible for communications, publications, maintenance, periodic review at least once per year, and eventual sunsetting as e needed. How governance dey interact with ADR? Consider areas like your organization ways of working, any special compliance needs like for legal aspects or human resource aspects, how you want handle consensus versus conflict versus escalation. Areas or people or teams dey wey fit get more influence pass others regarding ADR, like to fit approve am, or vote on am, or veto am? Example answer: Di governance of ADR dey for dis priority order: di CEO, di CTO, di CLO, di team wey implement ADR, di experts for di team wey know di AD pass. No one else get governance unless dem describe am for di ADR. Which principles dey interact with ADR? Consider areas like your organization ways of working wey include to move quickly versus to move slowly, for decision consensus versus decision conflict, and for risk preferences versus safety preferences, public discussion versus private discussion, and di like. Example answer: We dey use di leadership principles of bias for action, disagree-and-commit, 70% estimates dey good enough for easily-reversable easily-isolatable decisions, and public ways of working except confidential information as our organization confidentiality agreement describe.

records.title: wetin-be-architecture-decision-record
records.text: Wetin be architecture decision record? Architecture decision record (ADR) na document wey dey capture important architectural decision wey dem make together with im context and consequences. Architecture decision (AD) na software design choice wey address significant requirement. Architecture decision log (ADL) na di collection of all ADR wey dem create and maintain for particular project (or organization). Architecturally-significant requirement (ASR) na requirement wey get measurable effect on software system architecture. All dis one dey inside di topic of architecture knowledge management (AKM). Di goal of dis document na to give fast overview of ADR, how to create dem, and where to look for more information. Abbreviations: AD : architecture decision ADL : architecture decision log ADR : architecture decision record AKM : architecture knowledge management ASR : architecturally-significant requirement

headings: Architecture Decision Record fo Amazon Web Services
records.text: Architecture Decision Record fo Amazon Web Services Title: To Adopt Amazon Web Services fo Cloud Infrastructure Decision After thorough evaluation of various cloud infrastructure platforms, we don decide say our organization go adopt Amazon Web Services (AWS) for our cloud infrastructure needs. Background Our organization dey grow fast and we need reliable and scalable cloud infrastructure to meet di demands of our business. After we consider plenty cloud infrastructure providers, we conclude say AWS offer di most suitable range of services to meet our current and future requirements. Considerations Plenty cloud infrastructure providers dey for market wey don prove say dem reliable and efficient. But AWS no only offer comprehensive set of services to cater to our needs, e still get extensive customer base and track record of successful deployments. AWS also provide broad range of support and training resources to make sure say our team fit work effectively with di platform. Plus, AWS get extensive global presence with data centers for different regions around di world. Dis one ensure say our data secure and our applications and services go dey highly available. AWS also get robust security framework wey critical for our business. Lastly, AWS provide pay-as-you-go model wey give us flexibility to scale our infrastructure based on demand. Dis mean say dem go only charge us for wetin we use, wey allow us optimize our costs and invest for other areas of di business. Decision Based on di evaluations wey we perform and di advantages wey AWS offer, we don decide say we go adopt AWS for our cloud infrastructure needs. Consequences To adopt AWS fit require training for our teams to make sure say dem familiar with di platform and fit use am effectively. E fit also get some initial costs to move our current infrastructure go di AWS platform. Ownership Di cloud infrastructure team go dey responsible to make sure say dem use AWS effectively and to manage di risks wey associate with am. Dis team must address any issues wey arise. Review Dem go review di decision to adopt AWS every year to make sure say e still meet our needs and say dem dey fully realize di benefits of di platform.

records.title: Architecture Decision Record: API wey use JSON vs. gRPC
headings: Architecture Decision Record: API wey use JSON vs. gRPC
records.text: Architecture Decision Record: API wey use JSON vs. gRPC Status Accepted Context We dey design API for new service wey multiple clients go use. We don dey consider two options to implement di API: to use JSON over HTTP or to use gRPC. JSON over HTTP na widely-used approach to build APIs, and plenty programming languages and frameworks support am. Dis approach simple, lightweight, and easy to understand, so e be good choice for many projects. But e fit less efficient pass other options, especially wen e come to handle large amounts of data. gRPC, for di other hand, na newer technology wey offer more efficient way to build APIs. E dey use binary serialization to transfer data, wey fit faster and more compact than to use JSON. gRPC also support bidirectional streaming, so e be good choice for real-time applications. Decision After we consider di pros and cons of both options, we don decide to use gRPC for our API. Even though JSON over HTTP na simpler option, we believe say gRPC go give more efficient and scalable solution for our service. We also expect say our API go handle large amount of data, and gRPC binary serialization go more efficient for dis use case. Plus, we believe say gRPC support for bidirectional streaming go benefit real-time applications wey we fit develop for future. Consequences If we choose gRPC, we go need to use different set of tools and libraries to build our API compared to JSON over HTTP. Dis one fit require additional time and effort to learn and implement dis technologies. Also, clients wey want use our API go need to use gRPC-compatible libraries, wey fit no get as much support as JSON over HTTP libraries. But we believe say di benefits of to use gRPC pass dis potential drawbacks, and we confident say dis decision go result for more efficient and scalable API.

records.title: browser-automation-framework-fo-e2e-testing-playwright-vs-selenium
headings: Architecture decision record: browser automation framework fo E2E testing (Playwright vs Selenium)
records.text: Architecture decision record: browser automation framework fo E2E testing (Playwright vs Selenium) Context We dey di process to select browser automation framework for our end-to-end (E2E) testing pipeline. Dis framework go be integral to our CI/CD processes, to run tests wey simulate real user interactions on our platform. Specifically, di tests go cover scenarios like user sign-up/sign-in, file uploads, dashboard interactions, and report downloads. As startup , our focus na agile development , and we need to iterate and evolve rapidly. Our team mostly dey work with TypeScript and Python , and di ability to write tests for dis languages essential. Plus, di platform get interactive charts and dashboards , wey make am critical say di automation tool support rich, dynamic UIs well. Di two contenders for dis task na Playwright and Selenium , each get im strengths and trade-offs. We need to evaluate dis frameworks based on di features and requirements wey dem outline below. Considered Options Playwright (by Microsoft) Selenium (by the Selenium Project) Decision Drivers Di factors wey dey influence our decision na dis ones: Agile Development : Di tool wey we choose must enable fast, flexible development cycles. Language Support : Our team require support for both TypeScript and Python . Interactive UI Testing : Di ability to test interactive charts, dashboards, and dynamic elements reliably essential. Runtime Speed : Even though e no be primary concern, performance for CI/CD pipelines na consideration. Scalability : We no dey plan for massive scaling for di immediate future, but we want make sure say di solution fit handle future growth. Backwards Compatibility : Legacy systems and compatibility with older browsers no critical for our project at dis time. Mobile Testing : Even though e no be immediate focus, di framework suppose fit test mobile-responsive features or e suppose extensible for such use cases. Multi-monitor Testing : Support for multi-monitor configurations na secondary requirement, especially if we ever scale to testing for more complex user workflows. File Upload Testing : Di framework must handle file uploads efficiently, na core requirement of our testing needs. Evaluation Criteria Ease of Use : E easy to write and maintain tests? Language Support : Di framework support TypeScript and Python, di two languages wey our team dey use most frequently? Interactive UI Testing : How well di framework handle complex, interactive user interfaces like charts, file uploads, and dynamic data? CI/CD Integration : How well di framework integrate into common CI/CD tools and services? Cross-browser Support : Which browsers dem support and how well dem perform? Performance and Speed : How quick tests dey run, especially for CI/CD pipeline? Scalability : How well di framework fit scale if dem add more tests or more complex scenarios? Community and Ecosystem : How active di framework community be? Plenty integrations and extensions dey available? Considerations 5.1 Playwright Pros : Smarter API for Local File Uploads : Playwright API to interact with local files and to perform file uploads simpler and more intuitive. Dis one go make file upload testing easier to implement and maintain. Syntax and Code Generation : Playwright get shorter, more concise syntax. Dis one result for less boilerplate code, wey improve maintainability and developer efficiency. Plus, dis shorter syntax improve OpenAI code generation quality, wey make am easier to automatically generate test scripts. Interactive UI Testing : Playwright excel for testing dynamic, interactive web applications, like those wey get rich charts, complex user interactions, and real-time updates. E handle WebSockets, WebRTC, shadow DOMs, and other modern web technologies very effectively. Cross-browser Support : Playwright support Chromium , WebKit , and Firefox . E get consistent performance across dis browsers, wey suppose cover most of our testing needs. CI/CD Integration : Playwright integrate seamlessly with modern CI/CD platforms (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, etc.). E fit run tests for parallel across different browsers, wey optimize test run times and make am suitable for rapid development. Fast and Reliable : Playwright faster than Selenium in general, especially for headless mode, and e more resilient wen e dey deal with asynchronous web elements. Cons : Limited Mobile Testing : Even though Playwright support mobile emulation for browsers, e lack native mobile testing capabilities like Selenium integration with Appium for true mobile testing. Smaller Ecosystem : Playwright still newer and less established than Selenium. Even though e get rapidly growing community and good documentation, e fit never get di vast ecosystem of plugins and integrations wey Selenium offer. Limited Browser Support : Even though Playwright cover di major modern browsers (Chrome, Safari, Firefox), im support for legacy browsers (e.g., Internet Explorer) no robust as Selenium own. 5.2 Selenium Pros : Longer History and Maturity : Selenium don dey around for long time and e get proven track record. Plenty teams and industries dey use am widely, wey lead to vast ecosystem of plugins, integrations, and resources. Cross-browser and Cross-platform Support : Selenium support wide variety of browsers and versions, including Internet Explorer , and dem fit also integrate am with various tools like Docker , Selenium Grid , and cloud services for distributed testing. Mobile Testing : Selenium, through im integration with Appium , much more robust for mobile testing, including both Android and iOS applications. Dis one make am di better choice for projects wey get mobile-first or mobile-heavy focus. Multi-monitor Testing : Selenium provide better support for scenarios wey involve multiple monitors or complex multi-window interactions. Cons : Complexity : Selenium API more verbose and explicit. Even though dis one fit be advantage for some cases, e mean more code to write and maintain, wey fit reduce developer agility—especially important for startup environment. headings: Architecture Decision Record: How to Choose Database Technology
records.text: Architecture Decision Record: How to Choose Database Technology Status Accepted Context We dey design new application wey need to store and retrieve data in scalable and performant way. We don identify three types of database technologies wey people commonly use: relational databases, document databases, and event databases. Relational databases dey store data for tables with fixed schemas and dem enforce strict data integrity constraints. Dem suit applications wey need complex data relationships and transactions. Examples include MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle. Document databases dey store data for JSON-like documents and dem be schema-less. Dem suit applications wey need flexible data models and to scale horizontally. Examples include MongoDB, Couchbase, and Amazon DynamoDB. Event databases dey store data as series of events, wey capture every change to di data. Dem suit applications wey need auditing, event sourcing, and complex data processing. Examples include Apache Kafka, Apache Pulsar, and AWS Kinesis. Decision After we carefully evaluate di requirements and constraints of our application, we don decide to use document database. Rationale We choose document database because: Our application need flexible data model wey fit evolve as time dey go. Document databases allow us to store data for schema-less format, wey mean say we fit add new fields or change di structure of documents wey dey already without to modify di database schema. Our application need to scale horizontally to handle large volumes of data and traffic. Document databases provide built-in support for sharding and replication, wey enable us to distribute data across multiple servers and handle high read and write throughput. Our application need fast and efficient data retrieval. Document databases provide powerful indexing and querying capabilities wey enable us to retrieve data quick and efficiently. Our application no need complex transactions or data relationships. Even though relational databases excel to enforce data integrity constraints and to handle complex transactions, our application no get such requirements. Document databases fit provide sufficient consistency and durability guarantees for our use case. Consequences If we choose document database, we go need to invest for learning and understanding di specific technology wey we choose to use. Also, we go need to make sure say our application data model fit well with di data model of di document database to maximize performance and scalability. But we believe say di benefits of to use document database pass di costs, and say na di best fit for our application requirements and constraints.

records.title: Format fo timestamp
records.text: Format fo timestamp Wetin Dey Inside: Summary Issue Decision Status Details Wetin We Assume Wetin Dey Limit Us Positions Argument Wetin E Mean Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join Requirement Dem Wey Join Artifact Dem Wey Join Principle Dem Wey Join Notes Summary Issue We want fit track wen things happen by to use timestamps and by to use consistent timestamp format wey work well across all our systems and third-party systems. We dey interact with systems wey get different timestamp formats: JSON messages no get native timestamp format, so we need to choose how to convert timestamp to string, and convert string to timestamp, i.e. how to serialize/deserialize. Some applications set to use local time, instead of UTC time. Dis one fit convenient for projects wey must adjust to local time, like projects wey trigger events wey base on local time. Some systems get different time precision needs and capabilities, like to use time resolution of seconds vs. milliseconds vs. nanoseconds. For example, Linux operating system date command use default time precision of seconds, while Nasdaq stock exchange want default time precision of nanoseconds. Decision We choose di timestamp standard format ISO 8601 with nanosecond precision, specifically "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.NNNNNNNNNZ". Di format show di year, month, day, hour, minute, second, nanoseconds, and Zulu time zone a.k.a. UTC, GMT. Status Decided. Details Wetin We Assume We need to handle dis timestamp text strings, to convert from timestamp to string (a.k.a. serialize) and convert from string to timestamp (a.k.a. deserialize). We want format wey generally easy to use, easy to convert, and easy for person to read. We want compatibility with wide range of external systems wey we no fit control, like analytics systems, database systems, financial systems. Wetin Dey Limit Us Some systems get time precision limitations. For example, macOS operating system date command fit print time precision for seconds, but no for nanoseconds. Positions We consider range of options: Unix epoch i.e. one incrementing number. Terse text format "YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSNNNNNNNNN". To use local time zone vs. di UTC time zone. Argument For typical use, we value easy to read/write by humans, pass raw speed/size. For typical use, we want format wey work fine for machine systems, and also work well manually, like to write sample data, read JSON output, grep log file, etc. For atypical use, like high performance computing, we expect say we go want optimize any text format wey we choose by to convert di text to faster format, like programming language built-in date object type. So di text format no matter much for HPC. Wetin E Mean Our various text systems and time systems go converge on dis format. Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join We fit want fast/easy way to also track time deltas a.k.a. durations. Dem easy with Unix epoch timestamps. Requirement Dem Wey Join We fit want adjust our decision e.g. if we get related requirement for specific kind of logging message stamp, like for Splunk, Sumo, ELK, etc. Artifact Dem Wey Join Language formatters and parsers: date-fns: Modern JavaScript date utility library Crono: date and time library for Rust Rosetta Code examples: System time Data format Show the epoch SixArm examples: now string Principle Dem Wey Join Easily reversible. We fit change easy go different format, like Unix epoch. Defer premature optimization. For typical use we no care much about handful of extra characters like format wey use dashes and colons. Notes Add notes here.

Dis one dey accelerate di feedback loops. We fit swap in/out pieces from alternate vendors i.e. we fit want bring our own higher-speed build servers, or use our own choice of version control system, or coordinate with self-hosted continuous integration server. Streamlined usabilitiy na significant help, for developer experience, and in turn for subtle areas like consistency, clarity, security, and ease of learning curve. Wen anything break or get problem, we want effective way to report di issue. Dis one important especially for any security-related issues. Wetin Dey Limit Us None wey we know. Azure get published commitment to play well with external tools. Positions We consider to use Microsoft Azure Devops vs. AWS wey be incumbent. We experiment with Azure DevOps, Azure Pipelines, Azure Repo, and Azure spin up of new server through Terraform. We experiment to get support from Microsoft representatives. We gather information from peers on blogs and Hacker News. Argument Azure DevOps advertise excellent set of offerings, but dem no hold up, and dem no work well together, and support poor. Our firsthand experience: Azure setup na mess of UIs, some of dem overlap with Microsoft accounts, some no overlap. E.g. Azure sign in dey, Microsoft.com sign in dey, Live.com sign in dey, etc. and all of dem dey play at di same time. We meet minor security issue during setup, and we no find resolution. We try many ways to report am, to many Microsoft reps, with no success. We successfully report am to Microsoft security, wey reply with won't fix. Documentation often wrong or outdated. At least some of dis one na because of Microsoft poor search engine, and some na because of sub-par SEO. Terraform setup well documented, and e work. But Terraform supoprt weak compared to AWS because Microsoft dey build business relationships with vendors to do chain-through Terraform setup examples. Our peer experiences: After we do our own blind assessment, we look for peer experiences. Wetin we find confirm our experiences. Peers report additional problems with build times, and problems with bring-your-own-build server. Dis problems significantly more severe than UI problems, because to do builds na di core purpose of build pipeline, and we expect to do many per day. We find excellent participation by Azure teammates for di discussion areas. Kudos to Microsoft for dis. We impressed especially with Edward Thomson, Azure PM and coder, because of im participation, directness, and technical explanations. Wetin E Mean To choose Microsoft Azure DevOps look likely to cost more ( 3x) for time and cost than to no choose Azure. Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join If we choose Azure DevOps, many related offerings dey, including Azure Repo, Azure Pipeline, etc. We believe say if we choose Azure Devops, dis fit make am easier to use more Azure capabilities, or fit make am harder to use other vendors capabilities. We believe say Microsoft dey make great strides for developer experience, and we dey see Microsoft make large acquisition of developer tools (e.g. GitHub) and dependencies (e.g. Citus). If we choose Azure DevOps, then we fit want emphasize to choose di Microsoft acquisition offerings, and we fit also want approach di acquisition offerings with more care/assessement because of potential tissue-rejection e.g. staff turnover risk. Requirement Dem Wey Join We want make build times very fast. We accept to pay high premium for dis. Na because we want iterate very fast. We want make reliability very high. We accept to pay high premium for dis. Na because we dey test high-value use cases, including financial transations, confidential transactions, etc. Our top 4 devops KPIs include mean time to recovery, wey necessitate fast builds and high reliability. Artifact Dem Wey Join We want make di build system output artifacts wey suitable to use for other systems, like Artifactory. Principle Dem Wey Join Easily reversible. We fit evaluate Azure DevOps for parallel with AWS incumbent. Notes Microsoft Devops CI: Adventure Wey No Satisfy https://toxicbakery.github.io/vsts-devops/microsoft-devops-ci/ Blog post. "As software developer, I know first-hand how e hard to build quality products quick and cheap. Na art form wey we sometimes get right, and other times e dey turn into something like di Obama era healthcare government site. Our level of control over di product wey come out dey vary, and blame for failure often dey fall on di wrong people for di decision-making hierarchy. Microsoft Azure DevOps (wey dem before call Visual Studio Team Services), even though di intentions clear say dem good, na perfect storm of bad decisions and poor execution." Highlights from Hacker News discussion https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=18983586 "We dey use Azure DevOps extensively for my work and, after we don use GitHub, Gitlab, self hosted solutions, Jenkins, TeamCity... Azure DevOps rank dead last." "Di UI clunky terribly everywhere. Di worst for me na pull requests. E incredibly tough to work with people on pull request. I no fit even point you to "one" particular problem - for us e broken everywhere." "Azure Devops na something wey I want love. "We try also use Azure Boards (Work Items, Boards, Backlogs, etc). Ouch. Na complete UI mess of disjointed ideas. Instead of to implement one thing well, dem implement two dozen things terribly." Windows Development MVP Windows Development MVP dey here. I feel say I must carry some of di responsibility here because I no talk louder about dis issues. But I must talk say, I disappointed to hear say you "surprised" about di UX issues. I don dey tell your people say di UX dreadful (e.g. from as far back as pre-launch) and I keep hear back "we know, we dey fix am". I go start to formalize di feedback and push am through di pipes, stay tuned. I dey local too (Bellevue), I go like come in and try to pipeline our relatively simple oss .net/wpf/uwp app. I suspect say e go open eye for both of us. Some examples: You no fit build pipeline with git repo. wey get submodules I find say e impossible to edit di PATH for some custom tooling Di New Pipeline experience no make plenty sense, new users wey dey click around go eventually end up for di wrong Docs. Summary from Edward Thomson (Azure PM) Na me write di code wey merge your pull requests. records.text: Architecture Decision Record: Microsoft Azure cloud infrastructure" Decision Title: To adopt Microsoft Azure as di cloud infrastructure for our organization Decision Maker: Chief Information Officer Date: 2021-10-15 Status: Approved Background Di organization dey plan to migrate from traditional on-premises infrastructure go cloud infrastructure. To achieve dis, di organization don evaluate multiple cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud Platform (GCP), Microsoft Azure, and IBM Cloud. Each provider get im own set of features, benefits, and pricing structure. After detailed analysis, dem conclude say Microsoft Azure na di most suitable option for our organization. Decision Adopt Microsoft Azure as di cloud infrastructure for our organization. Rationale Na dis be di reasons to adopt Microsoft Azure: Comprehensive Services: Azure provide complete range of cloud services from infrastructure as a service (IaaS) to software as a service (SaaS) and platform as a service (PaaS). Dis one enable us to leverage Azure services to solve di organization requirements, like storage, compute, networking, and analytics. Scalability and Flexibility: With Azure, we fit easily scale up or down resources based on our business requirements. Azure also offer flexibility to choose di operating system, programming language, and frameworks. Security and Compliance: Azure offer high level of security and compliance, because e comply with several industry standards like ISO, SOC, HIPAA, and PCI DSS. Azure also provide advanced security features like network security groups, firewalls, and DDoS protection. Hybrid Cloud: Azure provide seamless hybrid cloud experience, wey enable organizations to connect their on-premises infrastructure with Azure. Dis one make am easy for us to migrate workloads go di cloud and e give us flexibility to choose where to store data. Cost-effective: Azure offer pay-as-you-go pricing model, wey mean say we only pay for di resources wey we use. Dis one help us save costs when we compare am to traditional on-premises infrastructure. Conclusion To adopt Microsoft Azure as di cloud infrastructure for our organization align with our business requirements and e offer several benefits like scalability, flexibility, security, and cost-effectiveness. So, dem recommend say make we adopt Azure as our cloud infrastructure.

records.text: Monorepo or multirepo Wetin Dey Inside: Summary Issue Decision Status Details Wetin We Assume Wetin Dey Limit Us Positions Argument Wetin E Mean Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join Requirement Dem Wey Join Artifact Dem Wey Join Principle Dem Wey Join Notes Summary Issue Our project involve to develop three major categories of software: Front-end GUIs Middleware services Back-end servers Wen we dey develop, our source code management (SCM) version control system (VCS) na git. We need to choose how we go use git to organize our code. Di top-level choice na to organize as "monorepo" or "polyrepo" or "hybrid": Monorepo mean say we put all pieces inside one big repo Polyrepo mean say we put each piece inside im own repo Hybrid mean some mix of monorepo and polyrepo For more, abeg check https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/monorepo-vs-polyrepo Decision Monorepo wen organization/team/project relatively small, and rapid iteration get higher priority than to sustain stability. Polyrepo wen organization/team/project relatively large, and to sustain stability get higher priority than rapid iteration. Status Decided. We open to revisit if/wen new tooling dey available to manage monorepos and/or polyrepos. Details Wetin We Assume All di code wey we dey develop na for one organization offerings, no be for general public. I.e. di Broker-Dealer no dey aim to get anything like general public volunteer developers. Wetin Dey Limit Us Dem document constraints well for https://github.com/joelparkerhenderson/monorepo-vs-polyrepo Positions We consider monorepos for di style of Google, Facebook, etc. We think say any monorepo scaling issues far for future so by di time we need dem, we go fit leverage di same practices as Google and Facebook. We consider polyrepos for di style of typical Git open source projects, like Google Android, Facebook React, etc. We think say na dem be di best choice for general public participation (e.g. anybody for di world fit work on di code) and individual availability (e.g. dem use di project on its own, without any other pieces). Argument Wen organization/team/project relatively small, we choose monorepo, because rapid iteration get significantly higher priority than to sustain stability Wen organization/team/project relatively large, we choose polyrepo, because to sustain stability get significantly higher priority than rapid iteration. Wetin E Mean If pipeline for CI+CD dey already, then we fit need to adjust am to test multiple projects inside one repo. CI+CD fit take more time for full build for monorepo, because CI+CD fit build all di projects inside di monorepo. If organization/team/project grow, then monorepo go get scaling issues. Monorepo scaling issues fit make am increasingly valuable to transition go polyrepo. Transition from monorepo go polyrepo na significant devops task, and dem go need to plan am, manage am, and program am. Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join We go create decisions for related tooling to manage monorepos (e.g. Google Bazel) and polyrepos (e.g. Lyft Refactorator). Requirement Dem Wey Join We need to develop di CI+CD pipeline so e go work well with git. Artifact Dem Wey Join We expect say di repo organization go get related artifacts for provisioning, configuration management, testing, and similar devops areas. Principle Dem Wey Join Easily reversible. If di monorepo no work for practice, or leadership no want am, e simple to change go polyrepo. Customer Obsession. We value to put di project for customers hands, and we believe say monoreop fit take us there faster than polyrepo, and also help us iterate faster. Think big. Google and Facebook strongly advocate for monorepos over polyrepos, because dem fit develop/test/deploy all di core offerings together. Notes Add any notes here.

records.text: Programming languages Wetin Dey Inside: Summary Issue Decision Status Details Wetin We Assume Wetin Dey Limit Us Positions Argument Wetin E Mean Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join Requirement Dem Wey Join Artifact Dem Wey Join Principle Dem Wey Join Notes Summary Issue We need to choose programming languages for our software. We get two major needs: front-end programming language wey suitable for web applications, and back-end programming language wey suitable for server applications. Decision We dey choose TypeScript for di front-end. We dey choose Rust for di back-end. Status Decided. We open to new alternatives as dem arise. Details Wetin We Assume Di front-end applications na typical: Typical users and interactions Typical browsers and systems Typical developments and deployments Di front-end applications likely to evolve quick: We want ensure fast easy developments, deployments, iterations, etc. We value provability, like type safety, and we dey fine to do small more work to achieve am. We no need legacy compatibility. Di back-end applications na higher-than-typical: Higher-than-typical goals for quality, especially provability, reliability, security, etc. Higher-than-typical goals for near-real-time, i.e. we no want pauses because of virtual machine garbage collection. Higher-than-typical goals for functional programming, especially for parallelization, multi-core processing, and memory safety. We accept lower compile-time speeds for favor of compile-time safety and runtime speeds. Wetin Dey Limit Us We get strong constraint on languages wey usable with major cloud provider services for functions, like Amazon Lambda. Positions We consider dis languages: C C++ Clojure Elixir Erlang Elm Flow Go Haskell Java JavaScript Kotlin Python Ruby Rust TypeScript Argument Summary per language: C: we reject am because of low safety; Rust fit do nearly everything better. C++: we reject am because e be mess; Rust fit do nearly everything better. Clojure: excellent modeling; best Lisp approximation; great runtime on di JVM. Elixir: excellent runtime including deployability and concurrency; excellent developer experience; relatively small ecosystem. Erlang: excellent runtime including deployability and concurrency; challenging developer experience; relatively small ecosystem. Elm: e look very promising; IBM dey publish major case studies with good results; smaller ecosystem. Flow: interesting improvement over JavaScript; but; developers dey move comot from am. Go: excellent developer experience; excellent concurrency; but e get track record of bad decisions wey cripple di language. Haskell: best functional language; smaller developer community; e never achieve enough published production successes. Java: excellent runtime; excellent ecosystem; sub-par developer experience. JavaScript: most popular language ever; most widespread ecosystem. Kotlin: e fix so much of Java; excellent backing by JetBrains; good published cases of porting from Java go Kotlin. Python: most popular language for systems administration; great analytics tooling; good web frameworks; but Google abandon am for favor of Go. Ruby: best developer experience ever; best web frameworks; nicest community; but very slow; somewhat hard to package. Rust: best new language; zero-abstraction emphasis; concurrency emphasis; but relatively small ecosystem; and e get deliberate limits on some kinds of compiler accelerations e.g. direct memory access need to be explicitly unsafe. TypeScript: e add types to JavaScript; great transpiler; growing developer emphasis on porting from JavaScript go TypeScript; strong backing from Microsoft. We decide say VMs get set of tradeoffs wey we no need right now, like additional complexity wey provide runtime capabilities. We believe say two cross-cutting concerns drive our core decision: For fastest runtime speed and tightest system access, we go choose JavaScript and C. For close-to-fastest runtime speed and close-to-tightest system access, we choose TypeScript and Rust. Honorable mentions go to di VM languages and web frameworks wey we go choose if we want VM language: Clojure and Luminus Java and Spring Elixir and Phoenix Wetin E Mean Front-end developers go need to learn TypeScript. Dis one likely easy learning curve if di developer primary experience na to use JavaScript. Back-end developers go need to learn Rust. Dis one likely moderate learning curve if di developer primary experience na to use C/C++, and hard learning curve if di developer primary experience na to use Java, Python, Ruby, or similar memory-managed languages. TypeScript and Rust both relatively new. Dis mean say many tools never get documentation for dis languages. For example, dem go need to set up di devops pipeline for dis languages, and so far, none of di devops tools wey we dey evaluate get default examples for dis languages. Compile times for TypeScript and Rust quite slow. Some of dis fit be because di languages new. We fit want look at how to mitigate slow compile times, like by compile-on-demand, compile-concurrency, etc. IDE support for dis languages never ubiquitous and never first-class. For example, JetBrains dey sell di PyCharm IDE for first-class support for Python, but e no dey sell IDE with first-class support for Rust; instead, JetBrains fit use Rust plug-in wey provide perhaps 80% of Rust language support vis a vis Python language support. Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join We go aim toward ecosystem choices wey align with dis languages. For example, we want choose IDE wey get good capabilities for dis languages. For example, for our front-end web framework, we more-likley to decide on framework wey tend to aim toward TypeScript (e.g. Vue) pass framework wey tend to aim toward plain JavaScript (e.g. React). Requirement Dem Wey Join Our entire toolchain must support dis languages. Artifact Dem Wey Join We expect say we fit export some secrets go environment variables. Principle Dem Wey Join Measure twice, build once. We dey prioritize some safety over some speed. Runtime more valuable pass compile time. We dey prioritize customer usage over developer usage. Notes Any notes here.

records.text: Architecture Decision Record: Rust programming language Decision Number: AR-001 Decision Title: How We Adopt Rust programming language Date: December 1, 2021 Status: Accepted Problem Statement As we dey continue to develop software applications, we don observe say e dey increasingly challenging to mitigate potential security vulnerabilities and prevent runtime errors. With di existing programming languages, like C and C++, we dey continue to experience issues like buffer overflows, memory leaks, and undefined behavior wey dey lead to crashes for applications. We require programming language wey provide memory safety guarantees and efficient enough to support performance-critical applications. Considerations Several programming languages dem design to address di existing problems. Among dem, Rust programming language don gain significant attention from developers community because of im unique design features. Considerations include; Memory safety and security Performance and efficiency Community support and adoption Learning curve Tools and ecosystem Compatibility with existing software systems. Constraints To adopt new programming language require retraining developers, wey take time and resources. E fit be challenge to integrate di language into di existing development workflow. We must ensure compatibility with di existing systems and avoid breaking changes so we go maintain continuity. Implementation Our development team go undergo training to learn and familiarize themselves with Rust programming language. We go create new project with Rust on trial basis to evaluate im compatibility and suitability for our development purposes. We go gradually migrate existing systems wey dem write for C and C++ go Rust. We go collaborate with Rust community to explore di tools and libraries wey dey available wey fit enhance our development workflow. We go monitor di performance of Rust and compare am to di performance of di existing programming languages regularly. We go adopt long-term approach wey balance di costs of training, integration, and potential benefits of to use Rust. Rationale We don adopt Rust because of im unique features wey dem design to provide memory safety and security guarantees while e still maintain performance and efficiency. Rust robust type system, borrow checker, and memory safety concepts make am highly suitable to develop performance-critical and safety-critical applications. Plus, Rust get significant community of developers, wey enable us to access wide range of tools, libraries, and ecosystem wey support our development workflow. Even though Rust come with learning curve, we believe say di benefits of to adopt Rust pass di costs and e provide excellent opportunity for continued growth and innovation. Consequences Di adoption of Rust go require significant investment of time and resources to train developers and integrate di language into di existing development workflow. To adopt Rust fit cause some degree of compatibility issues with existing systems, wey require refactoring, and modifications. Rust adoption fit increase di number of developers wey fit contribute to our project by to attract Rust developers wey want work on exciting projects. Di adoption fit lead to improved performance, efficiency, and safety compared to di existing languages. records.text: Architecture Decision Record: snake case v. camelCase fo REST API? Decision: Dem go use snake case naming convention for REST API endpoints Status: Accepted Context For naming conventions for REST APIs, two popular formats dey: snake case and camelCase. For snake case format, underscores dey separate each word for di name, while for camelCase, di first word of di name dey lower case, and di subsequent words get capital letter for their first letter. Dis decision go determine which naming convention suppose dem use for REST API. Decision Drivers Consistency with existing naming conventions for di project Readability and clarity for anybody wey fit dey work on di API Alignment with industry best practices for REST API naming conventions Ease of implementation and maintenance Decision Dem go use snake case naming convention for REST API endpoints. Na dis factors drive dis choice: Consistency : Di project already dey use snake case naming convention for all endpoints, and e go beneficial to maintain dis convention so e go ensure consistency across di whole project. Readability and clarity : Di snake case convention more readable and easier to understand. Di underscores provide clear separation between words, wey make am easier to parse and understand di meaning of di name. Alignment with industry best practices : Dem widely use snake case convention for di industry and dem consider am as best practice for REST APIs, wey make am good choice for di project. Ease of implementation and maintenance : To keep di existing naming convention easier to implement and maintain because dem go need to update all existing code and documentation if dem choose new convention. Consequences Potential consequences dey for dis decision. If any new team members wey join di project no familiar with snake case naming convention, e fit lead to confusion and mistakes for development. But since dem widely use snake case convention, such risk minimal. If dem use other tools or frameworks for di project wey heavily base on camelCase convention, e fit require extra effort to convert between naming conventions. Best For : Small-to-medium projects wey require utility-first, customizable approach. Table/Chart Support : Minimal. Grid/Gantt Support : Minimal. records.title: Architecture Decision Record: ways fo do authentication and authorization
headings: Architecture Decision Record: ways fo do authentication and authorization
records.text: Architecture Decision Record: ways fo do authentication and authorization Web application authentication and authorization na two crucial concepts to secure access to applications and services. Both deal with di identity of users and how dem dey grant permissions, but dem focus on different aspects: Authentication na di process to verify di identity of user or system. Authorization na di process to determine which resources or actions di authenticated user or system fit access. Now, make we enter di specific protocols and technologies wey you mention, wey dem commonly use for modern web applications to manage authentication and authorization. OAuth (Open Authorization) OAuth na open standard for authorization. E allow user to grant third-party application limited access to their resources without to share their credentials. Di key idea na delegated access . Dem often use OAuth for situations where users fit log in to third-party service (e.g., to sign in with Google) without to give their username and password direct to di third-party. Flow : OAuth typically follow token-based flow, where authorization server issue access token to di third-party application. Dis token represent di user permissions, and di application dey use am to access di user data or resources from API. Example : User sign into third-party app with their Google account. Google verify di user identity and then grant token wey allow di third-party app to access some Google data (e.g., Google Calendar). OAuth no dey handle authentication direct; na about to grant access. For authentication, dem often pair OAuth with other protocols, like OpenID Connect . OpenID Connect (OIDC) OpenID Connect (OIDC) na identity layer wey dem build on top of OAuth 2.0 wey add authentication to OAuth authorization capabilities. Essentially, OpenID Connect extend OAuth to handle user authentication and e give standardized way for applications to verify di identity of user. Flow : Wen user log in with OpenID Connect, di third-party application request ID token (plus di OAuth access token). Di ID token contain information about di user (like their username, email, and other claims). Dis one allow di application to know who di user be and whether dem authenticated. Example : To log into service like Slack with your Google account (Google na di OpenID Connect provider) involve authentication through OpenID Connect, while OAuth manage di access to your Google resources. OIDC make am easier for third-party apps to authenticate users while e still allow fine-grained control over which resources dose apps fit access. SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) SAML na older, XML-based standard wey dem use to exchange authentication and authorization data between parties, particularly for Single Sign-On (SSO) scenarios. Dem primarily use am for enterprise environments to enable users to authenticate once and access multiple applications without to enter credentials again. Flow : Di user first authenticate with identity provider (IdP). Di IdP generate signed SAML assertion wey include di user identity and related attributes. Dem send di assertion to di service provider (SP), wey use am to authorize access to di application. Example : Employee log into their corporate portal (di IdP) and dem automatically log am into other systems like email, CRM, etc., without to enter credentials again. Di authentication process base on di SAML assertion wey di IdP send. Dem commonly use SAML for enterprise SSO solutions and e work well for web applications for corporate environments, but e less mobile-friendly compared to OAuth/OIDC. WS-Federation (Web Services Federation) WS-Federation na another protocol wey dem use for Single Sign-On (SSO) , especially for Microsoft-based enterprise environments. E dey part of di WS- (Web Services) family of specifications and e allow identity federation across different security domains (like between different organizations or between different services). Flow : WS-Federation allow trusted identity provider (IdP) to authenticate users and issue tokens wey di service provider fit use for authorization. E similar to SAML but dem often use am for scenarios wey depend plenty on Microsoft technologies. Example : User log into enterprise application wey Microsoft Azure Active Directory (AD) host, and dem fit use their identity to access other federated services, including applications wey third-party vendors host. Even though newer protocols like OAuth2.0 and OpenID Connect largely replace WS-Federation for many modern web environments, dem still dey use am for legacy systems, especially for Microsoft-centric enterprises. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) LDAP na protocol wey dem use to access and manage directory services, commonly use to store user credentials and to manage access control for centralized directory (wey dem often call Directory Service ). LDAP no be specifically about authentication or authorization but dem use am to store and retrieve identity data, wey dem then use for dose processes. Authentication : LDAP allow application to authenticate users by to query di directory service for credentials (like passwords). Authorization : E also manage user roles and permissions, wey help determine whether user get access to certain resources. Example : Many enterprises dey use LDAP-based directories (e.g., Active Directory ) for authentication and authorization, especially inside Windows environments. LDAP crucial for enterprises to manage user access across internal systems, but for modern web context, dem often integrate LDAP with other protocols like SAML or OAuth for more complete identity management. Social SSO Providers Social Single Sign-On (SSO) providers like Facebook , Google , Twitter , GitHub , and others allow users to authenticate into third-party applications with their social media credentials. Dis na one type of OAuth-based authentication where di third-party service (e.g., Google) na di identity provider. Flow : Di user click "Log in with Google" (for example). Di app redirect go Google, where di user log in (if e never log in already). Google then give access token or ID token to di third-party app, wey dem fit use to authenticate di user and possibly access their data. Example : Many applications allow you to log in with your Google or Facebook credentials. Di app go use OAuth or OpenID Connect for background to verify your identity and, for some cases, access certain social media data. Social SSO na convenient and widely adopted method for authentication because e reduce friction for users, wey fit no want create another username and password again. --- Summary of Differences: OAuth : Dem use am for authorization, e allow third-party apps to access user data without to expose credentials. OpenID Connect : E extend OAuth to provide authentication, so apps fit verify user identity. SAML : XML-based protocol wey dem use for SSO, often for enterprise environments. WS-Federation : Microsoft-specific protocol for identity federation, wey dem use for legacy systems. LDAP : Protocol to query directory services to authenticate users and manage authorization. Social SSO Providers : OAuth-based systems (like Google, Facebook) wey allow third-party apps to authenticate users with their social media credentials. Each of dis technologies get im own strengths and use cases, and for modern applications, you fit see combination of dem wey dem dey use for different aspects of security (e.g., OAuth/OIDC for API access, SAML for enterprise SSO).
