headings: Architecture Decision Record: web application framework, batteries included, full stack, fo startup product
records.text: Architecture Decision Record: web application framework, batteries included, full stack, fo startup product Primary Objective: To build web application wey paying customers go use to sign in, upload files, process data, and view reports, wey focus on agile development, full-stack functionality, and strong compatibility with AI/ML tools, especially Project Jupyter notebooks. Context and Requirements: Agile Development (High Priority) : As startup, we need rapid iteration and flexibility. Agile practices, like quick prototyping, iterative development, and adaptability to change, na key to our development cycle. Full-Stack Framework (High Priority) : We aim to minimize overhead by to select framework wey fit handle both backend and frontend efficiently, so we go reduce di need for separate front-end frameworks. Compatibility with AI/ML Tools (High Priority) : Di ability to integrate easily with data analysis tools like Jupyter notebooks and Python data science ecosystem (NumPy, Pandas, TensorFlow, etc.) essential. Dis one go make efficient data processing and reporting easy. Low Importance Criteria : Runtime Speed : Even though performance relevant, e no be di most critical factor for di start because we care more about development speed and feature completeness. Scalability : We expect growth, but we fit address scalability concerns later, and e no be primary requirement right now. Backwards Compatibility : We dey focus on current technologies and we no too concern about backward compatibility with legacy systems. Frameworks Evaluated: Django (Python) Ruby on Rails (Ruby) Phoenix (Elixir) Loco (Rust) --- Django (Python) Overview : Django na high-level web framework for Python wey promote rapid development and clean, pragmatic design. People know am for im “batteries included” philosophy, wey mean say e include many features like authentication, routing, ORM, and form handling right out of di box. Strengths : Full-Stack : Django na comprehensive, full-stack framework wey fit handle both backend and frontend needs with integrated features (e.g., templating engine, admin interface). Agile Development : Django well-defined structure and conventions allow rapid development and adaptability, wey crucial for startup environment. Di framework come with excellent documentation and rich ecosystem of third-party packages, wey accelerate development. AI/ML Integration : Python ecosystem unmatched wen e come to data science and machine learning. Django, since e base on Python, integrate seamlessly with tools like Jupyter notebooks, Pandas, NumPy, TensorFlow, and scikit-learn. Community and Ecosystem : Django get extensive community, robust documentation, and wide range of plugins and extensions, wey significantly speed up development and troubleshooting. Weaknesses : Runtime Speed : Python tend to slower compared to languages like Rust or Elixir. But for dis use case, where performance no be primary concern, dis fit no be dealbreaker. Scalability : Even though Django highly scalable, challenges fit dey at very high scale without careful optimization (e.g., wen e dey handle heavy concurrent requests). But dem fit still scale Django effectively with load balancing and caching techniques. Verdict : Django align well with di requirements for agile development, full-stack support, and AI/ML compatibility. Im Python integration offer seamless access to di data science tools and libraries wey di application need. --- Ruby on Rails (Ruby) Overview : Ruby on Rails (RoR) na mature, full-stack web application framework wey people know for im convention-over-configuration approach, wey facilitate rapid development. Strengths : Full-Stack : RoR come with built-in tools for both backend and frontend development (e.g., views, templates, scaffolding), and im rich library of gems allow quick implementation of various features. Agile Development : People know Ruby on Rails particularly for im fast iteration cycles, wey advantageous for startups wey wan quickly iterate on features. RoR support test-driven development (TDD) and e get established ecosystem for agile workflows. Community and Ecosystem : RoR get well-established, strong community and wide array of gems wey fit speed up development. Ease of Use : Rails get very developer-friendly syntax and people know am for how e dey make tasks like database migrations, model-view-controller (MVC) architecture, and route handling quick and simple. Weaknesses : Performance : Ruby tend to get slower runtime performance compared to Python or Elixir. Even though RoR fit scale with di right infrastructure, Ruby performance fit become bottleneck for applications wey require heavy real-time processing or high concurrent traffic. AI/ML Integration : Even though Ruby get some machine learning libraries, dem no widely adopt am for di AI/ML community as Python. Integration with tools like Jupyter notebooks no too seamless, wey make Python stronger choice for data-heavy applications. Verdict : Even though Ruby on Rails excel for agile development and rapid prototyping, e fall short for terms of AI/ML compatibility compared to Python (Django). E viable choice for startups wey prioritize fast iteration over deep data analysis integration. --- Phoenix (Elixir) Overview : Phoenix na web framework wey dem build with Elixir, functional programming language wey dem design for scalability and concurrency. Phoenix leverage di Erlang VM, wey people know for how e dey handle massive concurrency and fault-tolerant systems. Strengths : Scalability and Performance : Phoenix shine for scalability and how e dey handle high concurrency. Dem build am on di Erlang VM, wey fit support thousands (or even millions) of concurrent connections, wey make am strong candidate for applications wey require real-time data processing or high-volume traffic. Full-Stack : Phoenix include everything wey dem need to build both di backend and frontend of application. E support live views for interactive UI updates and e include templating engine. Agile Development : Phoenix highly modular, wey allow rapid iteration on features. E well-suited for startups wey need to move quick. AI/ML Compatibility : Even though Elixir get emerging machine learning libraries, dem no support am widely for AI/ML tasks as Python. To integrate with tools like Jupyter notebooks go require workarounds, because Elixir ecosystem for data science no mature as Python own. Weaknesses : AI/ML Ecosystem : Elixir no be di primary language wey dem use for data science or machine learning, and di ecosystem no mature as Python own. So, integration with tools like Jupyter notebooks or popular AI libraries (TensorFlow, PyTorch) go cumbersome. Learning Curve : If di team no familiar with functional programming and Elixir, steeper learning curve fit dey. Verdict : Phoenix na excellent choice if scalability and concurrency na primary concern. But since AI/ML compatibility get priority, Phoenix fit no be di best fit because of Elixir limited ecosystem for dis space. --- Loco (Rust) Overview : Loco na web framework wey dem build with Rust, systems programming language wey people know for im performance, memory safety, and concurrency. Rust dey increasingly popular to build high-performance applications. Strengths : Performance : Rust primary strength dey for im high performance and memory safety, wey make am excellent choice for applications wey require low-level control or extremely high performance. Concurrency : Rust ownership system ensure memory safety while e allow safe concurrent programming, wey make am ideal for systems wey need to scale efficiently and handle parallelism. Weaknesses : Full-Stack Development : Loco, even though e promising, no mature as di other frameworks for terms of to provide complete full-stack solution. E more suitable for backend development, and di front-end ecosystem around Rust still dey emerge. Agile Development : To develop with Rust fit slower compared to higher-level languages like Python or Ruby because of im lower-level nature and steeper learning curve. AI/ML Ecosystem : Rust no get di same extensive ecosystem for AI/ML as Python. Even though growing libraries dey for Rust for numerical computing, dem far less mature than Python offerings, like Jupyter notebooks or machine learning frameworks. Verdict : Even though Rust and im framework Loco offer exceptional performance, di lack of full-stack support, agile development benefits, and AI/ML ecosystem make am less ideal for dis specific use case. E more suited for performance-critical applications instead of rapid web development with integrated data science tools. --- Conclusion After we evaluate di options based on di project requirements, Django (Python) na di most suitable choice. E offer dis advantages: Full-Stack Capabilities : Django na full-stack framework wey integrate both backend and frontend development. Agile Development : Di framework well-suited to rapid prototyping and iteration, wey essential for startup environment. AI/ML Compatibility : Python na di leading language for AI/ML, and Django compatibility with libraries like Jupyter notebooks ensure smooth integration for data analysis and processing. Community and Ecosystem : Django strong community support and extensive library ecosystem provide numerous tools to accelerate development. Even though Ruby on Rails also strong contender for agile development, im limited AI/ML support make am less ideal for dis specific use case. Phoenix (Elixir) and Loco (Rust) , even though dem excellent for scalability and performance, dem fall short for AI/ML integration and full-stack development. So, Django na di recommended framework for dis project.

records.text: Where to keep secret Wetin Dey Inside: Summary Issue Decision Status Details Wetin We Assume Wetin Dey Limit Us Positions Argument Wetin E Mean Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join Requirement Dem Wey Join Artifact Dem Wey Join Principle Dem Wey Join Notes Vault wey HashiCorp mek LastPass Bitwarden EnvKey Confidant wey Lyft mek Devolutions Password Server Secret Server wey Thycotic mek Summary Issue We need to store secrets, like passwords, private keys, authentication tokens, etc. Some of di secrets na user-oriented. For example, our developer want fit use their mobile phone to look up password to service. Some of di secrets na system-oriented. For example, our continuous delivery pipeline need fit look up di credentials for our cloud hosting. Decision Bitwarden for user-oriented secrets Vault by HashiCorp for system-oriented secrets. Status Decided. We open to new alternatives as dem arise. Details Wetin We Assume For dis purpose, and our current state, we value user-oriented convenience, like mobile apps wey usable. We want ensure fast easy access on di go, like for developer wey dey do on-call system reliability engineering. We want fit share some secrets among selected people, like team. We no dey try solve for single-provider, like to store all secrets exclusively on Amazon or Azure or Google. We no want ad-hoc approaches like "remember am" or "write am on note" or "figure out your own way to store am". Our security model for dis purpose dey fine with to use well-respected COTS vendors, like SaaS password management tools. Wetin Dey Limit Us Right now we want something wey easy i.e. no need to write code, no need to install servers, no need to make major commitment, no need to standardize everybody. Positions We consider: User-oriented off-the-self password managers: LastPass, 1Password, Bitwarden, Dashlane, KeePass, pass, GPG, etc. System-oriented COTS password managers: AWS KMS, Vault by HashiCorp, EnvKy, Secret Server by Thycotic, Devolutions Password Server, Confidant by Lyft. Sharing-oriented approaches: to use shared Google document, or shared Slack channel, or shared network folder, etc. Low-tech ad-hoc approaches, like to remember, to write note, or to rely on each user to figure out their own approach. Argument Bitwarden, LastPass, 1Password, and Dashlane all na commercial off-the-shelf products. Similar kinds of features for users, teams, organizations, etc. Desktop capability for Windows and Mac, and mobile capability for Android and iOS. Browser extensions for Chrome and Firefox, for automatic form fill in, etc. Bitwarden get two advantages over di others: Bitwarden na open source, wey mean say peers fit review di security and also security-oriented developers widely appreciate di company. Anecdotes by software workers describe significant preference for Bitwarden over di others. Typical good example writeup: https://jcs.org/2017/11/17/bitwarden Typical side-by-side voting site: https://stackshare.io/stackups/bitwarden-vs-dashlane We defer KeyPass, pass, GPG, etc. because additional complexity dey. All of dem look like fine solutions for technical users. GPG look especially good for technical users wey want cross-system command-oriented capabilities. We defer KMS because e get single-provider lock-in. We choose Vault for system-oriented needs, because di reviews amazingly positive, and because HashiCorp get excellent track record fup top-quality software and support. We veto di approaches of sharing approaches like through shared documents, shared channels, shared network folders, etc. Dem no provide di security qualities wey we want. We veto di ad-hoc low-tech approaches, because all of us agree say e no be long-term path forward. Wetin E Mean Developers fit need to track secrets for two places: Bitwarden for user-oriented access, and Vault for system-oriented access. Wetin Join Decision Dem Wey Join Di decision of which CI/CD server must include proof of capability to access secrets. We go need to decide how to managea di secrets, for terms of policies, rotations, organizations, etc. Requirement Dem Wey Join Di secrets go get related requirements for compliance, auditing, and HR onboarding/offboarding. Artifact Dem Wey Join We expect say we fit export some secrets go environment variables. Principle Dem Wey Join Easily reversible. Easily parallel i.e. e easy to use variety of password managers. Cheap to try i.e. free trial dey and no commitment. Notes Evaluation notes here. Di notes all na public comments on various devops discussion boards. Vault wey HashiCorp mek Vault na exactly wetin you want here. No just throw Vault go production though, stand am up for test environment first, because HashiCorp documentation fit lack plenty even if their products amazing. Very steep learning curve and e no trivial to stand up. Di initial setup na small pain. E worth am well though, and di community go support am well enough for you to get by. Horrid docs but plenty guides dey online of people wey set am up and if you put few of dem together you go get working setup. Initial setup take fiddling with their helm charts (vault and consul). While technically you fit use plenty other back-ends, I really really no recommend am. Di back-end/consul fit be teeny tiny if you no get ton of data to store. Definitely get comfortable/familiar with how to use di CLI, because di GUI na more like proof-of-concept/advertisement portal for their enterprise edition. Di fact say you no fit just "fill am up" na pain. For example if you get 5 fields you need to manually add each field for each item. So e no be like say you pre-define fields for specific category, and fill those fields for all di items for dat category, e more like "you generate everything every time", wey (for my mind) na pain for di ass. You fit want also look at goldfish as UI for on top of vault. E make am rather nice to get your team on board with am. Dem get demo too. 1. Set up consul. 2. Set up vault wey point to consul. 3. Set up goldfish wey point to vault. 3. Setup some cron job to run consul snapshot for backups. LastPass LastPass Teams. We dey use am, e get custom templates, ACL, nothing missing IMO. I implement LastPass for my org and I give am C+/B-. Di biggest issue lately na lack of reliability. For di past 90 days multiple hours don dey wey dem force vaults go offline mode. Dis no ideal for my org because we get, literally, 4,000+ passwords wey dem store across 20+ shared folders. As you fit imagine with that many passwords at least few dey get updated or added daily. We get DR plan if issues last more than hour or two: script dey sign and encrypt CSV dump of vault every night wey fit import into keepass. LastPass don get unreported blips of degraded service: login 'works' but e no pull sites, random features broken for di admin panel, and e no share keys properly for new top level shared folders. I get specific 'key push'/backup user wey dey every group. Usually if you log in as dat user e go fix any key sharing issues but no wen di service degraded even though wetin di status page talk... For integration e fit easy if you get proper ACLs with least privileged model e.g. if user get read & write and read only on entry or folder dem go only get read only permissions. Unfortunately my org ACLs no too good so I end up use di JSON provisioning API and 500 lines of python because di dependent nature of our hundreds of ACLs no map well to di least privileged model. I end up get all ACLs wey user dey inside and do dependency walk of sorts. If your ACL or group structure don already build with least privileged structure for mind, di AD/LDAP sync tool for Windows go work well. Reach out to their sales team and dem fit hook you up with longer Enterprise trial. Make sure say you fully understand im limitations before you pull di trigger. We get good number of growing pains but apart from outages or impairments for di server side e don dey incredibly smooth. Bitwarden Bitwarden get nice tooling around am (WebUI, CLI, Mobile, Desktop). Self-hosted and fairly easy to setup. Fairly good documentation and PrivacyTools recommend di tool. EnvKey https://www.envkey.com/ Na saas. Really easy to implement, integrate and manage. Features: Protect API keys and credentials. Keep configuration in sync everywhere. Smart, end-to-end encrypted configuration and secrets management. Prevent insecure sharing and config sprawl. Integrate in minutes. Capabilities: Manage configuration and access levels for all your apps, environments, and teams for one place. Configure any development or server environment with just single environment variable. Pros: Good home page. Clear value prop. Visually excellent web app. Superior example data e.g. Algolia, AWS, Datadog, GitHub, Stripe, etc. I speak with di founder for 30m about di company, UI, etc. Dane sound well-informed, honest about di pros/cons, and viable partner. Di company na essentially typical Y Combinator company, with 1 founder. Dem raise $120K for 2018-01. Focus na to get to enterprise features, esp. to move from EnvKey cloud-hosting go either on-prem or BYOC. Potential path forward wey start with EnvKey for ease of use, then later (or for parallel) add Vault. Confidant wey Lyft mek https://lyft.github.io/confidant/ Confidant na open source secret management service wey provide user-friendly storage and access to secrets for secure way, from di developers for Lyft. KMS Authentication: Confidant solve di authentication chicken and egg problem by to use AWS KMS and IAM to allow IAM roles generate secure authentication tokens wey Confidant fit verify. Confidant also manage KMS grants for your IAM roles, wey allow di IAM roles generate tokens wey dem fit use for service-to-service authentication, or to pass encrypted messages between services. At-rest encryption of versioned secrets: Confidant dey store secrets for append-only way for DynamoDB, e dey generate unique KMS data key for every revision of every secret, with Fernet symmetric authenticated cryptography. User-friendly web interface to manage secrets: Confidant provide AngularJS web interface wey allow end-users easily manage secrets, di mappings of secrets to services and di history of changes. Devolutions Password Server https://server.devolutions.net/ Secure, manage, and monitor access to privileged accounts and sessions. Comprehensive, highly-secured password vault wey let you control access to your privileged accounts, while e also improve overall network visibility for sysadmins and provide seamless experience for end users. Features: centralized organization password vault, user-specific private vault, password manager, credential injection, Active Directory integration, role-based access control, two-factor authentication, enterprise ready, IP restrictions, management capabilities, automated password generator, mobile app access, password history, access reports, email alerts. e support data encryption e support multiple Authentication schemes including LDAP, O365, and Local users WITH support for MFA from multiple sources multiple repositories/vaults with fine-grained access controls for multiple teams modern Web UI private credential and connection vaults for personal creds/connections mobile apps for IOS/Android audit logs for each entry, who/what/when with optional prompt for why dem dey access am customizable templates (though dem support hundreds of connection types natively) tons more features and Windows/Mac thick client (Remote Desktop Manager) wey you fit sync to wey greatly expand di options...one-click connections pricing no too bad - up to 15 users na $500 a year for di password server Secret Server wey Thycotic mek https://thycotic.com/products/secret-server/ On-premise version features: Total control over your end-to-end security systems and infrastructure Deploy software inside your on-premise data center or your own virtual private cloud instance Meet legal and regulatory obligations wey require all data and systems to reside on premise Cloud version features: Software-as-a-service model let you sign up and start right away Elastic scalability as you grow Controls and redundancy wey Azure deliver with 99.9% uptime SLA User feedback: We dey use that product before. Dem easily bypass am and di rules only work for smart people. Lazy or dumb users fit easily screw am up for team area. Prices dey negotiable wen you talk to dem. You fit run am with SQL express and Win 7box. Cheap.

records.text: Decision record fo 4-day work-week Title: How to Implement 4-Day Work-week Context and Problem Statement Our organization don dey consider to switch go 4-day workweek. Di current work schedule of 5 days per week, 8 hours per day, don cause low productivity, employee burnout, and high turnover rates. Di change wey dem propose wan increase employee satisfaction, engagement, and retention, and finally improve organizational performance. Decision We don decide to implement 4-day workweek starting from di next quarter for all employees across di organization. Rationale Dem base di decision on dis factors: Employee feedback: Survey wey dem conduct among di employees show say dem want more flexible work schedule and better work-life balance. Di majority of di respondents show interest for 4-day workweek. Research findings: Studies on companies wey don implement 4-day workweek don show increased employee productivity, reduced absenteeism, and improved work-life balance. Competitive advantage: To offer 4-day workweek fit be attractive benefit to potential employees and e fit help retain talent wey we get already. Organizational goals: Di switch to 4-day workweek align with our organizational goals to create healthier and more productive work environment. Implementation Plan Dem go take dis steps to implement di 4-day workweek: Communication: Dem go communicate di decision to all employees through company-wide email and meeting with team leaders. Schedule: Di new schedule go be Monday to Thursday for full-time employees, with option of flexible schedules for part-time employees. Dem go extend work hours to 10 hours per day. Policy updates: Dem go update human resources policies, like leave policies and benefits, so dem go align with di new schedule. Training: Dem go train managers on how to manage teams under di new schedule and how to track employee performance and productivity well. Evaluation: Dem go evaluate di new work schedule after six months to determine im impact on employee satisfaction, engagement, and retention. Anticipated outcomes Dem expect say di implementation of 4-day workweek go produce dis outcomes: Increased employee satisfaction, engagement, and retention. Improved work-life balance for employees. Increased productivity and reduced absenteeism. More attractive employee benefit package and competitive advantage for di hiring market. Conclusion We believe say di implementation of 4-day workweek go benefit our organization and our employees. We dey look forward to see di positive impact of dis decision on our employees and our overall organizational performance.

records.text: Decision record fo work from home Title: Employees fit work from home Decision Maker: Management Team Decision Date: July 1, 2021 Background Because of di ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, many employees don dey work remotely from home. Dis arrangement don provide benefits like increased flexibility, improved work-life balance and decrease for how di virus dey spread. Plus, numerous employees don talk say dem go like continue to work from home even after di pandemic don end. Decision After dem weigh di pros and cons of to allow employees work from home, di management team don decide to implement permanent work from home policy for eligible employees. Di policy apply to all full-time employees wey fit effectively perform their duties from home and wey don show success to work remotely during di pandemic. Eligible employees fit choose to work from home up to three days per week, while dem go require in-office work for di remaining two days. To ensure effective communication and collaboration, dem go require regular check-ins with team members and managers. Plus, dem go provide employees with di necessary equipment and resources to perform their duties effectively from home. Dem go review and revisit di implementation of dis policy regularly to make sure say e still benefit both di employees and di company. Reasoning Di decision to continue to allow employees work from home base on several factors, including employee work-life balance, greater flexibility and freedom, improved productivity, and less exposure to di risk of infection. If di company implement flexible work model, e fit attract and retain top talent while e still provide positive company culture. Implications Di implementation of di permanent work from home policy go get several implications, including di need for ongoing communication and coordination among team members, to adjust work processes and protocols so dem go accommodate remote workforce, and to ensure say all employees get access to di necessary equipment, tools and resources. Conclusion Di decision to implement permanent work from home policy dey in line with di company values to promote healthy work-life balance, support employee well-being and promote positive company culture. We believe say dis decision go enable our organization to be more agile and better suited to adapt to changing business needs while e improve employee satisfaction and productivity.

records.text: Decision record templet wey arc42 mek Introduction and Goals Short description of di requirements, driving forces, extract (or abstract) of requirements. Top three (max five) quality goals for di architecture wey get highest priority for di major stakeholders. Table of important stakeholders with wetin dem expect regarding architecture. 1.1 Requirements Overview Contents Short description of di functional requirements, driving forces, extract (or abstract) of requirements. Links to di requirements documents (we hope say dem exist), with information where to find am. Motivation From di point of view of di end users, dem create or modify system to improve support of business activity and/or improve di quality. Form Short textual description, probably for tabular use-case format. If requirements documents exist, dis overview suppose refer to dem. Keep dis excerpts as short as e possible. Balance di readability of dis document with potential redundancy w.r.t. requirements documents. 1.2 Quality goals Content Di top three (max five) quality goals for di architecture wey di major stakeholders need dem to fulfill pass. We really mean quality goals for di architecture. No confuse dem with project goals. Dem no necessarily identical. Di ISO 25010 standard give nice overview of potential topics of interest. Motivation You suppose know di quality goals of your most important stakeholders, because dem go influence fundamental architectural decisions. Make sure say you be very concrete about dis qualities, avoid buzzwords. If you as architect no know how dem go judge di quality of your work … Form Table with di most important quality goals and concrete scenarios, wey dem order by priorities. 1.3 Stakeholder Content Explicit overview of stakeholders of di system, i.e. all person, roles or organizations wey suppose know di architecture dem must convince about di architecture must work with di architecture or with code need di documentation of di architecture for their work must come up with decisions about di system or im development Motivation You suppose know all parties wey dey involved for development of di system or wey di system affect. Otherwise, you fit get nasty surprises later for di development process. Dis stakeholders determine di extent and di level of detail of your work and im results. Form Table with role names, person names, and wetin dem expect regarding di architecture and im documentation. Constraints Anything wey constrain teams for design and implementation decisions or decision about related processes. E fit sometimes go beyond individual systems and e valid for whole organizations and companies. Content Any requirement wey constrain software architects for their freedom of design and implementation decisions or decision about di development process. Dis constraints sometimes go beyond individual systems and dem valid for whole organizations and companies. Motivation Architects suppose know exactly where dem free for their design decisions and where dem must adhere to constraints. Dem must always deal with constraints; but dem fit dey negotiable. Form Simple tables of constraints with explanations. If need dey, you fit subdivide dem into technical constraints, organizational and political constraints and conventions (e.g. programming or versioning guidelines, documentation or naming conventions) Context and Scope E dey delimit your system from im (external) communication partners (neighboring systems and users). E specify di external interfaces. Dem show am from business/domain perspective (always) or technical perspective (optional) Content System scope and context - as di name suggest - delimit your system (i.e. your scope) from all im communication partners (neighboring systems and users, i.e. di context of your system). So e specify di external interfaces. If necessary, differentiate di business context (domain specific inputs and outputs) from di technical context (channels, protocols, hardware). Motivation Di domain interfaces and technical interfaces to communication partners dey among di most critical aspects of your system. Make sure say you completely understand dem. Form Various context diagrams Lists of communication partners and their interfaces. 3.1 Business context Content Specification of all communication partners (users, IT-systems, …) with explanations of domain specific inputs and outputs or interfaces. Optionally, you fit add domain specific formats or communication protocols. Motivation All stakeholders suppose understand which data dem dey exchange with di environment of di system. Form All kinds of diagrams wey show di system as black box and specify di domain interfaces to communiations partners. Alternatively (or additionally) you fit use table. Di title of di table na di name of your system, di three columns contain di name of di communication partner, di inputs, and di outputs. 3.2 Technical context Contents Technical interfaces (channels and transmission media) wey link your system to im environment. Plus mapping of domain specific input/output to di channels, i.e. explanation of which I/O use which channel. Motivation Many stakeholders dey make architectural decision based on di technical interfaces between di system and im context. Especially infrastructure or hardware designers dey decide dis technical interfaces. Form E.g. UML deployment diagram wey describe channels to neighboring systems, together with mapping table wey show di relationships between channels and input/output. Solution Strategy Summary of di fundamental decisions and solution strategies wey shape di architecture. E fit include technology, top-level decomposition, approaches to achieve top quality goals and relevant organizational decisions. Contents Short summary and explanation of di fundamental decisions and solution strategies, wey shape di architecture of di system. Dis include technology decisions decisions about di top-level decomposition of di system, e.g. usage of architectural pattern or design pattern decisions on how to achieve key quality goals relevant organizational decisions, e.g. to select development process or to delegate certain tasks to third parties. Motivation Dis decisions na di cornerstones for your architecture. Dem be di basis for many other detailed decisions or implementation rules. Form Keep di explanation of dis key decisions short. Motivate wetin you decide and why you decide am dat way, based on your problem statement, di quality goals and key constraints. Refer to details for di following sections (section 5 for structural details, section 8 for crosscutting concepts). You fit use list of solution-approaches or table. Building Block View Static decomposition of di system, abstractions of source-code, wey dem show as hierarchy of white boxes (wey contain black boxes), up to di appropriate level of detail. Content Di building block view show di static decomposition of di system into building blocks (modules, components, subsystems, classes, interfaces, packages, libraries, frameworks, layers, partitions, tiers, functions, macros, operations, data structures, …) and also their dependencies (relationships, associations, …) Dis view na mandatory for every architecture documentation. If you compare am to house, na di floor plan. Motivation Maintain overview of your source code by to make im structure understandable through abstraction. Dis one allow you to communicate with your stakeholder for abstract level without to disclose implementation details. Form Di building block view na hierarchial collection of black boxes and white boxes (check di figure below) and their descriptions. 5.1 Whitebox Overall System Here you describe di decomposition of di overall system wey use di following white box template. E contain overview diagram motivation for di decomposition black box descriptions of di building blocks wey dey inside. For dis one we offer you alternatives: use one table for short and pragmatic overview of all di building blocks wey dey inside and their interfaces use list of black box descriptions of di building blocks according to di black box template (check below). Depending on di tool wey you choose, dis list fit be sub-chapters (for text files), sub-pages (for Wiki) or nested elements (for modelling tool). (optional:) important interfaces, wey no dey explained for di black box templates of building block, but wey very important to understand di white box. Since plenty ways dey to specify interfaces, we no provide specific template for dem. For di best case, examples or simple signatures go be enough. 5.2 Level 2 Here you fit specify di inner structure of (some) building blocks from level 1 as white boxes. You must decide which building blocks of your system important enough to justify such detailed description. Abeg prefer relevance over completeness. Specify important, surprising, risky, complex or volatile building blocks. Leave out normal, simple, boring or standardized parts of your system 5.2.1 White Box for building block 1 E specify di internal structure of building block 1. Use di white box template (check above). Runtime View Behavior of building blocks as scenarios, wey cover important use cases or features, interactions for critical external interfaces, operation and administration plus error and exception behavior. Content Di runtime view describe concrete behavior and interactions of di system building blocks for form of scenarios from di following areas: important use cases or features: how building blocks dey execute dem? interactions for critical external interfaces: how building blocks dey cooperate with users and neighbouring systems? operation and administration: launch, start-up, stop error and exception scenarios Remark: Di main criterion to choose possible scenarios (sequences, workflows) na their architectural relevancy. E no important to describe large number of scenarios. Better you document representative selection. Motivation You suppose understand how (instances of) building blocks of your system dey do their job and communicate for runtime. You go mainly capture scenarios for your documentation to communicate your architecture to stakeholders wey less willing or able to read and understand di static models (building block view, deployment view). Form Many notations dey to describe scenarios, e.g. numbered list of steps (for natural language) activity diagrams or flow charts sequence diagrams BPMN or EPCs (event process chains) state machines etc. 6.n Runtime Scenario n (1, 2, 3, etc.) Insert runtime diagram or textual description of di scenario. Insert description of di notable aspects of di interactions between di building block instances wey di diagram depict. Deployment View Technical infrastructure with environments, computers, processors, topologies. Mapping of (software) building blocks to infrastructure elements. Content Di deployment view describe: di technical infrastructure wey dem use to execute your system, with infrastructure elements like geographical locations, environments, computers, processors, channels and net topologies and also other infrastructure elements and di mapping of (software) building blocks to dat infrastructure elements. Often dem dey execute systems for different environments, e.g. development environment, test environment, production environment. For such cases, you suppose document all relevant environments. Especially document di deployment view wen dem execute your software as distributed system with more than one computer, processor, server or container or wen you design and construct your own hardware processors and chips. From software perspective, e enough to capture dose elements of di infrastructure wey need to show di deployment of your building blocks. Hardware architects fit go beyond dat and describe di infrastructure to any level of detail wey dem need to capture. Motivation Software no dey run without hardware. Dis underlying infrastructure fit and go influence your system and/or some cross-cutting concepts. So, you need to know di infrastructure. Form Maybe di highest level deployment diagram don already dey inside section 3.2. as technical context with your own infrastructure as ONE black box. For dis section you go zoom into dis black box with additional deployment diagrams. UML offer deployment diagrams to express dat view. Use am, probably with nested diagrams, wen your infrastructure more complex. Wen your (hardware) stakeholders prefer other kinds of diagrams instead of UML deployment diagram, let dem use any kind wey fit show nodes and channels of di infrastructure. 7.1 Infrastructure Level 1 Describe (usually with combination of diagrams, tables, and text): di distribution of your system to multiple locations, environments, computers, processors, .. and also di physical connections between dem important justification or motivation for dis deployment structure quality and/or performance features of di infrastructure di mapping of software artifacts (building blocks) to elements of di infrastructure For multiple environments or alternative deployments, abeg copy dat section of arc42 for all relevant environments. 7.2 Infrastructure Level 2 Here you fit include di internal structure of (some) infrastructure elements from infrastructure level 1. Abeg copy di structure from level 1 for each selected element. Crosscutting Concepts Overall, principal regulations and solution approaches wey relevant for multiple parts (→ cross-cutting) of di system. Concepts often relate to multiple building blocks. Include different topics like domain models, architecture patterns and -styles, rules to use specific technology and implementation rules. Content Dis section describe crosscutting concepts (practices, patterns, regulations or solution ideas). Such concepts often relate to multiple building blocks. Dem fit include many different topics. Motivation Concepts form di basis for conceptual integrity (consistency, homogeneity) of di architecture. So, dem be important contribution to achieve inner qualities of your system. Dis na di place for di template wey we provide for cohesive specification of such concepts. Many of dis concepts relate to or influence several of your building blocks. Form Di form fit vary: concept papers with any kind of structure example implementations, especially for technical concepts cross-cutting model excerpts or scenarios wey use notations of di architecture views Structure of this section Pick only di most-needed topics for your system and assign each level-2 heading for dis section (e.g. 8.1, 8.2 etc). NO TRY to cover all di topics of di diagram wey we mention before. Background Some topics inside systems often concern multiple building blocks, hardware elements or development processes. E fit easier to communicate or document such cross-cutting topics for one central location, instead of to repeat dem in di description of di building blocks, hardware elements or development processes wey concern. Certain concepts fit concern all elements of system, others fit only be relevant for few. Architectural Decisions Important, expensive, critical, large scale or risky architecture decisions including rationales. Content Important, expensive, large scale or risky architecture decisions including rationales. With “decisions” we mean to select one alternative based on given criteria. Abeg use your judgement to decide whether architectural decision suppose be documented here for dis central section or whether e better to document am locally (e.g. inside di white box template of one building block). Avoid redundant texts. Refer to section 4, where you don already capture di most important decisions of your architecture. Motivation Stakeholders of your system suppose fit comprehend and retrace your decisions. Form ADR (architecture decision record) for every important decision list or table, wey dem order by importance and consequences or more detailed for form of separate sections per decision Background (on ADRs) Smaller pieces of documentation easier to read, create and maintain. Wen e come to architecture decisions, development teams often: know about di decision, as e visible e.g. for source code, but miss di motivation behind dat decision (check Nygard 2011) So you suppose document few important decisions together with their motivation, reasoning Our proposal concerning decisions Keep collection of architecturally significant decisions, dose decisions wey affect di structure, quality characteristics, important (especially external) dependencies and interfaces, or construction techniques (thanks to Michael Nygard for dis proposal). Quality Requirements Quality requirements as scenarios, with quality tree to give high-level overview. Di most important quality goals suppose don dey described for section 1.2. (quality goals). Content Dis section contain all relevant quality requirements. Dem don already describe di most important of dis requirements for section 1.2. (quality goals), so dem suppose only dey referenced here. For dis section 10 you suppose also capture quality requirements wey less important, wey no go create high risks if dem no fully achieve dem (but fit be nice-to-have). Motivation Since quality requirements go get plenty influence on architectural decisions, you suppose know which qualities really important for your stakeholders, for specific and measurable way. Further Information Check di extensive Q42 quality model for https://quality.arc42.org. 10.1 Quality Requirements Overview Content Overview or summary of quality requirements. Motivation Often we dey meet dozens (or even hundreds) of detailed quality requirements. For dis overview section, you suppose try to summarize, e.g. by to describe categories or topics (as ISO 25010:2023 or Q42 suggest If dis summary descriptions don already precise, specific enough and measurable, you fit skip section 10.2. Form Use simple table where each line contain category or topic and short description of di quality requirement. Alternatively, you fit use mindmap to structure dis quality requirements. For literature, dem don also describe di idea of quality attribute tree, wey put di generic term “quality” as di root and use tree-like refinement of di term “quality”. [Bass+21] introduce di term “Quality Attribute Utility Tree” for dis purpose. 10.2 Quality Scenarios Content Quality scenarios dey make quality requirements concrete and dem allow to decide whether dem fulfilled (for di sense of acceptance criteria). Make sure say your scenarios specific and measurable. Two kinds of scenarios dey especially useful: Usage scenarios (dem also dey call dem application scenarios or use case scenarios) describe di runtime reaction of di system to certain stimulus. Dis also include scenarios wey describe di efficiency or performance of di system. Example: Di system react to user request within one second. Change scenarios describe di desired effect of modification or extension of di system or of im immediate environment. Example: Dem implement additional functionality or requirements for quality attribute change, and dem measure di effort or duration of di change. Form Typical information for detailed scenarios include di following: For short form (wey Q42 model favour): Context/Background: Which kind of system or component, wetin be di environment or situation? Source/Stimulus: Who or wetin initiate or trigger behaviour, reaction or action. Metric/Acceptance Criteria: Response wey include measure or metric Di long form of scenarios (wey SEI and [Bass+21] favour) more detailed and include di following information: Scenario ID: Unique identifier for di scenario. Scenario Name: Short, descriptive name for di scenario. Source: Di entity (user, system, or event) wey initiate di scenario. Stimulus: Di triggering event or condition wey di system must address. Environment: Di operational context or condition wey di system experience di stimulus under. Artifact: Di building-blocks or other elements of di system wey di stimulus affect. Response: Di outcome or behavior wey di system show as reaction to di stimulus. Response Measure: Di criteria or metric wey dem use to evaluate di response of di system. See also Since January 2023, arc42 dey provide pragmatic quality model, wey propose to label quality requirements, with hashtags or labels like #flexible, #efficient, #usable, #operable, #testable, #secure, #safe, #reliable. Risks and Technical Debt Known technical risks or technical debt. Which potential problems dey inside or around di system? Wetin dey make di development team feel miserable? Content List of technical risks or technical debts wey dem identify, wey dem order by priority Motivation “Risk management is project management for grown-ups” (Tim Lister, Atlantic Systems Guild.) Dis suppose be your motto for systematic detection and evaluation of risks and technical debts for di architecture, wey management stakeholders (e.g. project managers, product owners) go need as part of di overall risk analysis and measurement planning. Form List of risks and/or technical debts, probably including suggested measures to minimize, mitigate or avoid risks or reduce technical debts.

records.text: {Your Title Here} !!! info Status : { Proposed Under Review Accepted Rejected Superseded Deprecated } Updated : {YYYY-MM-DD} Summary {Dis na di 'executive summary' or 'elevator pitch' for your ADR. For few concise sentences (typically 2-4), state clear di core problem, question, or opportunity wey dis ADR address. Include small hint of di decision wey dem make or di area of focus. Di goal na to help readers understand quick wetin dis ADR be about and decide if e relevant to dem, without to read di whole document. Think of am as di abstract of technical paper or very brief introduction to di main topic.} Drivers {Dis section dey explain why dem dey make dis decision now . Articulate clear di primary motivations, needs, or problems wey make dis architectural decision necessary. Think about di underlying reasons and pressures.} {e.g. We dey develop new feature/capability wey need...} {e.g. We need improve performance, accessibility, remove debt...} {e.g. Feedback from users suggest say...} {e.g. Di current approach impose dis limitations...} Options {Na here you go list di different options wey you dey consider. Stick to di facts and avoid opinions, di next section go cover di analysis. Include concise description, links to relevant documentation or examples. Include all significant alternatives wey you explore, even if dem finally no choose dem. Di goal na to give readers clear, unbiased understanding of each alternative before you enter di evaluation.} {Option 1 Title} {Describe di option, give summary, list di facts, provide links etc.} {Option n Title} ... Options Analysis {Na here you go critically evaluate each option wey dem present for di Options section. For each option, give balanced view of im advantages, disadvantages, and any other relevant considerations or trade-offs. Be specific and, where e possible, relate your points back to di Drivers . Consider aspects like: Cost (development, operational, licensing) Complexity (implementation, maintenance, learning curve) Risks (technical, operational, security) Alignment with architectural principles or existing standards Impact on performance, scalability, usability, maintainability, security, etc. Include as many Pro/Con/Other statements as e required. } {Option 1 Assessment} Pro: {Specific advantage or benefit of dis option.} Con: {Specific disadvantage, risk, or cost wey dey associated with dis option.} Other: {Relevant point wey no strictly pro or con.} {Option n Assessment} ... Recommendation {Na here you go state clear di final decision, and name explicit di option wey dem select. Explain in detail why dem choose dis option. You suppose articulate clear how di chosen option best address di Drivers and meet di key requirements or solve di problem wey dem state.} Consequences {Dis section na optional .} {Now wey dem don make decision, wetin be di expected outcomes and impacts, both positive and negative? Which known limitations, costs, or risks dem dey accept by to make dis decision? How dis decision go affect different stakeholders, other systems, development practices, operational procedures, or user experience?} Pro: {Specific positive outcome or benefit wey dem expect from dis decision.} Con: {Specific downside, cost, or risk wey dem accept wey result from dis decision. } Other: {Consequence wey no strictly pro or con.} Confirmation {Dis section na optional .} {Outline how dem go verify di implementation of dis decision and how ongoing compliance go dey ensured. Dis one dey help show say di decision no be just theoretical but dem go actively put am for practice and monitor am. How you go check say dem implement di decision correct? (e.g., code reviews, specific tests, demonstrations, peer review). How dem go maintain adherence to dis decision as time dey go? (e.g., automated checks, periodic audits, updates to team guidelines, training). Specific metrics or indicators dey wey go show say di decision dey achieve im intended positive outcomes? (e.g., performance benchmarks, adoption rates, reduction in specific errors, user feedback scores). Who responsible to oversee dis, and wetin go happen if dem no follow di decision?} More Information {Dis section na optional .} {Use dis section to give any supplementary information wey support di decision, add context, or guide future actions. Links to other decisions and resources fit appear here too. You fit note briefly who dey involved for di decision-making process and if/how dem reach consensus. You fit also want suggest timeframe or specific events wey fit prompt re-evaluation of dis decision for di future.}

records.text: Decision record templet wey Jeff Tyree and Art Akerman mek Dis na di architecture decision description templet wey dem publish for "Architecture Decisions: Demystifying Architecture" by Jeff Tyree and Art Akerman, Capital One Financial. Issue : Describe di architectural design issue wey you dey address, so no question go remain about why you dey address dis issue now. Follow minimalist approach, address and document only di issues wey need addressing at different points for di life cycle. Decision : State clear di direction of di architecture—dat na, di position wey you select. Status : Di status of di decision, like pending, decided, or approved. Group : You fit use simple grouping—like integration, presentation, data, and so on—to help organize di set of decisions. You fit also use more sophisticated architecture ontology, like John Kyaruzi and Jan van Katwijk own, wey include more abstract categories like event, calendar, and location. For example, if you use dis ontology, you go group decisions wey deal with occurrences where di system need information under event. Assumptions : Describe clear di underlying assumptions for di environment where you dey make di decision—cost, schedule, technology, and so on. Note say environmental constraints (like accepted technology standards, enterprise architecture, commonly employed patterns, and so on) fit limit di alternatives wey you consider. Constraints : Capture any additional constraints to di environment wey di chosen alternative (di decision) fit pose. Positions : List di positions (viable options or alternatives) wey you consider. Dem often need long explanations, sometimes even models and diagrams. Dis no be exhaustive list. But you no go want hear di question "Did you think about...?" during final review; dis one dey cause loss of credibility and questioning of other architectural decisions. Dis section also dey help make sure say you hear other people opinions; if you state other opinions explicit, e dey help enroll their advocates for your decision. Argument : Outline why you select one position, including items like implementation cost, total ownership cost, time to market, and availability of required development resources. Dis one probably important as di decision itself. Implications : Decision dey come with many implications, as di REMAP metamodel denote. For example, decision fit introduce need to make other decisions, create new requirements, or modify existing requirements; pose additional constraints to di environment; require renegotiating scope or schedule with customers; or require additional staff training. If you understand and state clear di implications of your decision, e fit very effective to gain buy-in and to create roadmap for architecture execution. Related decisions : E obvious say many decisions dey related; you fit list dem here. But we don find say for practice, traceability matrix, decision trees, or metamodels dey more useful. Metamodels dey useful to show complex relationships diagrammatically (like Rose models). Related requirements : Decisions suppose dey business driven. To show accountability, map your decisions explicit to di objectives or requirements. You fit enumerate dis related requirements here, but we don find say e more convenient to reference traceability matrix. You fit assess how each architecture decision contribute to meeting each requirement, and then assess how well dem meet di requirement across all decisions. If decision no contribute to meeting requirement, no make dat decision. Related artifacts : List di related architecture, design, or scope documents wey dis decision impact. Related principles : If di enterprise get agreed-upon set of principles, make sure say di decision consistent with one or more of dem. Dis one dey help ensure alignment across domains or systems. Notes : Because di decision-making process fit take weeks, we don find say e useful to capture notes and issues wey di team discuss during di socialization process.
